title: Host-side throttling and fragmentation cascade – lab notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick lab notes documenting a previously underexplored failure mode we saw in production: host-side allocation throttling (malloc/calloc/jemalloc) interacting with CUDA workspace patterns producing a fragmentation cascade and intermittent OOMs even when aggregate free memory looked sufficient. Goal is to capture hypotheses, traces to gather, and short experiments to triage.

Summary of observed symptom: 
- Customer cluster experienced transient OOMs on a multi-tenant Dedicated node during high KV-cache churn (frequent load/unload of cached past-key-values).
- GPU resident memory reported ~70–80% utilization with >10% free fragmentation pockets (via device free maps), but application-level CUDAMallocAsync calls failed with out-of-memory errors.
- Host-side dmesg and allocator logs showed a flurry of small host mallocs (tens to hundreds KB) immediately preceding GPU allocation failures.
- When we throttled host allocation rate (artificial sleep in host thread), GPU OOMs less likely, suggesting a host-side pressure -> device eviction/deferral interaction.

Key hypothesis (cascade): 
1) High KV-cache churn triggers many short-lived host allocations (scratch buffers, protobuf parsing, temporary pinned pages for transfers).
2) Host allocator (jemalloc or libc malloc) experiences fragmentation and internal caching growth; some frees are deferred by thread-caches, causing increased RSS and pinned memory footprint.
3) Pinned host pages and allocations used for cudaHostAlloc / cuMemHostRegister or implicit pinned staging cause the NIC/driver to reserve DMA-addressable regions; the driver then reports less available pageable memory for large contiguous cudaMalloc allocations.
4) CUDA runtime/driver falls back to slower allocation path (or to cudaMallocAsync arenas) which needs contiguous device memory; because device pools are fragmented under simultaneous stream activity, allocation fails even though total free bytes > requested size.
5) The result looks like an OOM at the device but root cause is cross-layer pressure originating on host-side allocation patterns.

Evidence we have so far: 
- CUPTI traces (stream timeline) show host thread allocations tightly correlated with device allocation failures (within 10–30ms).
- jemalloc stats (background sampling) show spike in thread cache refill and epoch counter increments at same time windows.
- NVidia driver logs show repeated fallback to synchronous alloc path and 'allocation retry' messages.
- Memory maps (pmap) show a cluster of recently committed anonymous mappings with high RSS around failure time.

Instrumentation to gather next: 
- Full allocation timeline (host + device) with microsecond resolution for a reproducer: wrap malloc/calloc/free, cudaHostAlloc/cuMemHostRegister, cudaMalloc/cudaMallocAsync, and cuCtxSynchronize.
- Export jemalloc stats (extent fragmentation counters, tcache hit/miss) at 100ms intervals during runs.
- GPU memory defragmentation heatmap: capture allocation/release addresses (virtual device pointers) and coalescing behavior from our runtime's pool manager.
- CUPTI/CUDA driver logs and nvprof sampling on a reproducer.
- OS-level pinned pages and mlocked pages (cat /proc/<pid>/smaps + grep "Pinned" where supported) — correlate with device allocations.
- NIC DMA mapping pressure counters where possible (driver-specific).

Repro recipe (local lab): 
- Workload: lightweight LLM inference loop with small-batch KV cache churn every 300–600ms. Use a model with large KV size (e.g., 32k context) and alternating requests that trigger cache insertions and evictions.
- Inject noisy host allocations in the same worker thread path: allocate many small buffers, then free them (simulate parser allocations).
- Run with two allocator configurations: system malloc and jemalloc with tcache disabled (MALLOC_CONF="tcache:false") and with tcache enabled.
- Run with cudaMallocAsync enabled vs disabled. Capture failure rate across runs.

Planned experiments and expected signals: 
1) Disable host-thread tcache (jemalloc) -> expected: less thread-local RSS but more malloc overhead; if OOM frequency drops, tcache deferred frees were contributing.
2) Force immediate host free coalescing (via madvise/MADV_DONTNEED or explicit free path) -> expected: improved contiguous host memory for pinned allocation, fewer cuda failures.
3) Reduce number of concurrent CUDA streams (serialize some work) -> expected: reduce interleaved allocation pattern and lower fragmentation.
4) Pre-reserve a host pinning slab for staging buffers (fixed-size pool) -> expected: reduce runtime pinning churn and stabilize driver DMA mappings.
5) Increase device pool slab sizes (favor larger contiguous blocks) -> expected: fewer allocation retries but higher steady GPU usage; tradeoff appraisal needed.
6) Add small sleep/backpressure on host allocation hot-path -> expected: reduce short-term pressure and give allocator time to reclaim.

Mitigations to prototype in runtime (short list): 
- Allocation batching for KV-cache: group frees for short-lived scratch and do them off the hot path (background reclaim thread).
- Host pin pool: centralize cudaHostAlloc/cuMemHostRegister usage into an arena with lease semantics so driver-visible pinning patterns are stable.
- Proactive defragmentation: periodic compaction of device workspace (move to free pool then coalesce) during low-load windows.
- Observability: expose per-request host pinned bytes, tcache pressure, and the runtime's allocator fragmentation ratio in Console dashboards and add SLO alerts for ephemeral pin spikes.
- Fallback policy: when GPU allocation fails, automatically attempt: 1) short exponential backoff + retry, 2) fall back to smaller model variant, 3) fail fast with richer diagnostics (dump small snapshot).

Open questions and unknowns: 
- How much of the driver-side allocation failure is due to pinned host memory vs purely device fragmentation? We need address mapping traces from the driver to be sure.
- Does NUMA placement of host pinned pages matter significantly for our workload? Reproducer should pin process to single NUMA node and test cross-node behavior.
- Are there kernel-level limits (e.g., max map count, vm.max_map_count) contributing? Check sysctl during tests.

Notes from quick smoke runs (2024-08-30 to 2024-09-02): 
- Run A (no tcache changes): 7 failures in 1k requests.
- Run B (tcache disabled): 1 failure in 1k requests.
- Run C (pre-reserve host-pin pool 32MB): 0 failures in 1k requests, but throughput dropped ~3%.
- Run D (cudaMallocAsync enabled): similar failure rate as baseline unless device pool slab size increased.

Immediate action items: 
- [Priya] Build an instrumented reproducer with allocation wrappers and upload CUPTI traces -> due 2024-09-06 (SRV-1289).
- [Ethan] Add jemalloc epoch snapshots to nightly stress harness and chart in Grafana -> due 2024-09-10.
- [Zoe] Prototype host-pin slab pool in branch and run perf/regressions -> due 2024-09-12.
- [Diego] Open kernel/driver ticket with NV support if we can reproduce with driver logs -> due 2024-09-08.

Longer-term items for RFC: 
- Design an allocator contract across layers (app -> host allocator -> pinned pool -> device pool) with clear visibility and backpressure signals.
- Add adaptive throttling in runtime: if host pinned usage crosses threshold, throttle noncritical background frees or delay cache inserts.

References and related tickets: 
- Related GHs in serving-runtime about cudaalloc retry behavior (see linked PR).
- Prior fragmentation notes in the directory (useful background but this file focuses on host->device cascade rather than pure device arena algorithms).

Appendix: quick commands used during experiments: 
- jemalloc stats: MALLOC_CONF=stats_print:true LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.2 (use env to dump epoch).
- gather pinned pages: sudo perf mem record or parse /proc/<pid>/smaps (Pinned: field where present).
- CUPTI capture: use cupy/cupti wrapper with timeline collection and correlate host timestamps to runtime logs.

End of notes.

(These are working notes — will iterate into a short RFC if experiments confirm the hypothesis.)
